html:
An epidemic of yellow fever in Philadelphia, then capital of the United States, from August to November 1793. About 5,000 or more people died, roughly a tenth of a city of some 50,000.

The disease likely came with refugees and ships from the Caribbean, where the Haitian Revolution was raging. Nobody then knew that mosquitoes spread it. About 20,000 people fled the city, among them President George Washington and much of the federal government.

Doctors fought over causes and cures. Benjamin Rush pushed heavy bleeding and purging, while others favoured rest. The Free African Society, led by Absalom Jones and Richard Allen, nursed the sick and buried the dead, on the false belief that Black people could not catch the fever; many of them died. The epidemic ended with the first frosts, which killed the mosquitoes. It pushed Philadelphia to build a public water system and a health board.
sum: An epidemic of yellow fever in Philadelphia, then capital of the United States, from August to November 1793. About 5,000 or more people died, roughly a tenth of a city of some 50,000.
